Himalayan vulture chicks hatch after an incubation period of 57 days [ab = 57 days] when nests are maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that reflects the substantial energetic demands of developing a large body within the egg. Upon hatching, the initial wet weight of a neonate averages 258 grams [Ww0 = 258 grams], a mass that is modest relative to the formidable size these birds ultimately attain. This hatchling mass represents the starting point for a growth trajectory that must support the rapid skeletal and muscular development required for flight and independent foraging. The precocial chicks are covered in dense down and are capable of limited movement shortly after emergence, though they remain entirely dependent on parental provisioning for warmth and nutrition. The 57-day incubation period at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] (57 days) [ab = 57 days] is consistent with that of other large Gyps species, where extended egg development is linked to the high calcium demands of forming a robust calcareous shell and a well-developed altricial-precocial intermediary chick. Field observations indicate that hatching success is closely tied to stable thermal conditions within the nest cavity, as fluctuations can prolong development or reduce neonate viability.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this scavenger, approximately 40 °C [T = approximately 40 °C], fledging occurs at 138 days after hatching [tx = 138 days after hatching]. This relatively extended nestling phase is characteristic of large soaring birds, allowing ample time for the complete development of flight feathers and the musculature necessary for sustained soaring flight. During this period, the chick experiences a dramatic increase in mass, transitioning from its initial hatchling weight toward the ultimate adult body mass. The age at first breeding is deferred considerably, with individuals typically initiating reproduction at 6 years after hatching [tR = 6 years after hatching] at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This delay in first reproduction is a common life-history strategy among long-lived raptors, where the benefits of early breeding are outweighed by the survival and competitive advantages gained through an extended period of somatic and social maturation before reproductive investment begins. The protracted pre-breeding phase allows young vultures to refine foraging techniques and establish dominance hierarchies at carcass sites, critical skills for securing adequate nutrition.

Sexual maturity, as indicated by the onset of gonadal activity and the development of secondary sexual characteristics, is attained at 414 days after hatching [tp = 414 days after hatching] at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This milestone occurs well after fledging but still considerably earlier than the first successful breeding event, underscoring a period of adolescent sterility typical of many avian species with complex social structures. The attainment of puberty does not immediately translate into reproductive output, as young birds must first secure a breeding territory and a mate within the competitive colony environment. Adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, for males reaches approximately 11,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 11,000 grams], a value that reflects the substantial dimorphism present in this species, with males typically outweighing females. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for the general population, representing a mix of sexes, is around 9,000 grams [Wwi = around 9,000 grams], though considerable individual variation exists based on local food availability and seasonal condition. This large body size imposes high absolute energetic demands, requiring efficient thermoregulation and the ability to exploit ephemeral carrion resources over vast home ranges.

The maximum reproductive rate, expressed through natural annual output, involves females producing a single egg per nesting attempt [N_R_i = a single egg per nesting attempt] each year, with one nesting event occurring annually [F_R_i = one nesting event occurring annually] and a maximum daily reproduction rate of 1 egg per year [Ri = 1 egg per year]. This low fecundity is a hallmark of k-selected life-history strategies, where parental investment per offspring is exceptionally high. The single chick is brooded intensively for the first several weeks and is provisioned with regurgitated carrion by both parents throughout the nestling period. This strategy of a single, well-provisioned offspring contrasts sharply with the multiple-egg clutches of smaller raptors and reflects the substantial resource investment required to fledge a large-bodied juvenile capable of surviving its first winter. The extended period of parental care, coupled with the deferred age at first reproduction, results in a slow population turnover rate that makes this species particularly vulnerable to elevated adult mortality from anthropogenic sources such as collision with power lines and poisoning at carcass dumps. Conservation efforts therefore focus heavily on reducing threats to adult survival to maintain viable population sizes.

Maximum recorded longevity in the Himalayan vulture, derived from banding studies and captive records conducted at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], is approximately 28.3 years [am = approximately 28.3 years]. This impressive lifespan places it among the longest-lived of the accipitrid vultures, a ranking that is consistent with its large body size and relatively slow pace of life. Such extended longevity allows individuals to accumulate substantial reproductive output over a lifetime, despite the constraints of a single-egg clutch and a delayed onset of breeding. The species exhibits negligible senescence until very late in life, with experienced adults maintaining high breeding success rates even at advanced ages. The substantial size differential between the sexes, where male Himalayan vultures reach an ultimate wet weight of 11,000 grams [Wwi = 11,000 grams], is consistent with a mating system that likely involves intense male-male competition for access to carcasses and nesting territories. The average adult body mass across both sexes is approximately 9,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 9,000 grams], as recorded in multiple field studies. These mass values are supported by measurements taken from wild individuals during routine trapping and monitoring efforts in the Himalayan foothills and the Tibetan Plateau.
